statements.text: Could I ask each of you to consider in the law enforcement arena what you believe to be the most promising use of AI that we in Congress should consider encouraging, [...] what you consider to be the most dangerous use of AI that we should be more closely monitoring?
statements.context: Senator Whitehouse poses a question to a panel of witnesses during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI in criminal investigations and prosecutions.

statements.text: One of the concerns that I have about the markets for AI tools is that most of the paying customers are law enforcement, and defense experts and defense investigators don't have the same money to throw at the problem. And this may bias the development of technologies in favor of identifying evidence of guilt rather than identifying evidence of innocence.
statements.context: Senator Whitehouse speaks during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on AI in criminal investigations and prosecutions.

statements.text: Question two is, are you working in the development of AI with some of the medical specialty groups—orthopedics, cardiologists—and do you think they are a useful place for either benchmarking or approval or somehow accrediting best AI practices?
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in health care where Senator Whitehouse poses written-for-the-record questions to an expert panel.

statements.text: I just wanted to find out from each one of you if you think that there is a particularly good source—like, for instance, New Hampshire's Attorney General—or a particularly good article or analysis on where gaps are in the criminal law that should be plugged, in order to deal with the problem of deliberate and malicious AI fakery.
statements.context: Senator Whitehouse questions witnesses during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI election deepfakes.

statements.text: Energy-hungry data centers and cryptomining facilities are overloading our already strained power grid, driving up consumers' electricity costs, making it harder for Americans to power their homes and businesses, and spiking fossil fuel emissions. [...] The good news is that we don't have to choose between leading the world on AI and leading the world on climate safety: big technology and AI companies have all the money in the world to pay for developing new sources of clean energy, rather than overloading local grids and firing up fossil fuel pollution.
statements.venue: Press release on Clean Cloud Act introduction (EPW minority)

statements.text: I am concerned by reports that Meta plans to power a data center in northeastern Louisiana with new and unabated natural gas generation. This flies in the face of Meta's climate commitments and its claims that it has achieved net zero emissions in its global operations.
statements.venue: Letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, quoted in EPW press release

statements.text: The artificial intelligence folks, the crypto folks, the data system folks who need massive amounts of electrons — you all need to start showing up and letting people know that you actually want permitting reform, and you actually want an administrative and regulatory process in which electrons are treated fairly, irrespective of source, so you can get the power that you need.
statements.venue: Senate floor remarks, reported by E&E News

statements.text: It could make a big difference if the AI, crypto and data people said, 'Wait a minute, we need these damn electrons.' They have not. They are just beginning to. We are seeing them for the first time in the permitting reform conversation.
